title: Without sound, without touch
theme: Having discerned that which is without sound, touch, form, taste or smell, unchanging and eternal, without beginning or end, beyond the great, steady — one is freed from the mouth of death.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «न व्येति न क्षीयते», it does not pass away or diminish
Raṅgarāmānuja: to be joined with each of the negatives, «प्रत्येकम् अभिसम्बध्यते»
Śaṅkara: «महत्तत्त्वाद्बुद्ध्याख्यात्»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the individual self of 1.3.13

sandhi.type: m before a vowel; m before a consonant
sandhi.rule: A final m before a vowel is kept and joined to it; before a consonant it becomes anusvāra, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
Like vowels join long, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
A final t becomes c before c, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः).
The final t stays before p.

samasa.meaning: without beginning and without end; Śaṅkara: «अविद्यमानः आदिः कारणमस्य तदिदमनादि», «अविद्यमानोऽन्तः कार्यमस्य तदनन्तम्»
that which has no sound; so also asparśam, arūpam, arasam

morphology.note: agandha, ‘without smell’, with the possessive -vat — literally ‘having no-smell’. Śaṅkara repeats it in his summary of the five: «अशब्दमस्पर्शमरूपमरसमगन्धवच्च यत्».
Masculine, though the relative yat and the adjectives are neuter: the neuter ‘that which’ is the masculine Self (Śaṅkara: «तम् आत्मानं»).
Absolutive of ni-√cāy, ‘perceive, discern’; the same form as in 1.1.17 (nicāyyemām, corrected there in this edition).

translation.literal: That which [is] soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal and smell-less, without beginning or end, beyond the great, steady — having discerned it, one is freed from the mouth of death.
translation.readable: What has no sound, no touch, no form, no taste and no smell, what does not decay and is eternal, without beginning or end, beyond the great and unmoving: one who discerns it is freed from the jaws of death.

anvaya: यत् अशब्दम् अस्पर्शम् अरूपम् अव्ययम् तथा अरसम् नित्यम् अगन्धवत् च [अस्ति], तम् अनाद्यनन्तम् महतः परम् ध्रुवम् निचाय्य मृत्युमुखात् प्रमुच्यते ।
syntax: A relative clause with yat and a string of neuter adjectives describes the object; the second line adds more qualifications in the accusative, takes it up with tam, and gives the result: nicāyya … pramucyate, ‘having discerned it, [one] is freed’. The subject of the passive is left unexpressed.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: beyond the principle called intellect, «महत्तत्त्वाद्बुद्ध्याख्यात्», as in 1.3.10–11. Raṅgarāmānuja: mahataḥ refers to the individual self named in 1.3.13 (‘the great self’): «इति पूर्वमन्त्रनिर्दिष्टो जीवो गृह्यते».
Śaṅkara: «अवगम्य», having understood. Raṅgarāmānuja: having made it an object by meditation like seeing, «दर्शन-समानाकारोपासनेन विषयीकृत्य इत्यर्थः».

beginner: Death now sums up what he has been describing. It has no sound, no touch, no shape, no taste and no smell: none of the five senses can find it. It does not wear away; it is eternal; it has no beginning and no end. It is beyond even the great principle at the top of the earlier ladder, and it stands still. Whoever comes to perceive it is freed from the mouth of death. Śaṅkara explains why the list of absences matters: everything we can sense is made of parts and changes, so what has none of those qualities cannot change or end. The mouth of death, he says, is ignorance, desire and the actions they produce. Raṅgarāmānuja takes the mouth of death as frightening saṃsāra, the round of birth and death, and the discerning as a meditation that sees it clearly.
analogy: Like describing space by what it is not — not wood, not stone, not water — until what is left is the room in which all of them stand.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It describes that which has none of the five qualities the senses perceive, which does not decay, is eternal, without beginning or end, beyond the great and fixed, and says that one who discerns it is freed from the mouth of death.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: why the absence of qualities makes it eternal
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Gross things are made of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, and as these fall away, from earth to space, things become subtler and more lasting. What has none of them is subtle without limit: «एतद्व्याख्यातं ब्रह्म». It does not decay because it has no such qualities, «इदं त्वशब्दादिमत्त्वादव्ययं न व्येति न क्षीयते», and it is eternal because it has no cause and no effect. It is beyond the great because it is consciousness itself, «नित्यविज्ञप्तिस्वरूपत्वात्», and steady because it is unchanging, «कूटस्थं नित्यं». The mouth of death is ignorance, desire and action: «मृत्युगोचरादविद्याकामकर्मलक्षणात्».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: each quality is eternal; the great is the self
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He reads the verse as a conclusion («उपसंहरति»). ‘Eternal’ goes with each of the negatives, «इत्यादौ प्रत्येकम् अभिसम्बध्यते», and the Supreme is undecaying like time, «कालवद् अव्ययम्». ‘The great’ is the individual self of 1.3.13, so the Supreme is beyond the self. To discern it is to make it an object by meditation like seeing, and the mouth of death is fearful saṃsāra: «भीषणात् संसारात् इत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The five negatives follow the five sense-qualities: sound, touch, form, taste, smell. Śaṅkara explains the list by the elements: earth has all five, and from water up to space each has one quality fewer and is correspondingly subtler and more lasting: «तत्रैकैकगुणापकर्षेण गन्धादीनां सूक्ष्मत्वमहत्त्वविशुद्धत्वनित्यत्वादितारतम्यं दृष्टमबादिषु यावदाकाशमिति». What has none of them is subtle without limit.

advaita.text: The verse defines Brahman by the absence of every sensible quality: «एतद्व्याख्यातं ब्रह्म»; knowing it as the Self frees one from ignorance, desire and action, the domain of death.

visistadvaita.text: The Supreme is beyond the individual self named ‘great’ in 1.3.13, and is reached by meditation like seeing: «दर्शन-समानाकारोपासनेन विषयीकृत्य इत्यर्थः»; the release is from saṃsāra.

schools.disagreement: Whether ‘beyond the great’ means beyond the cosmic intellect, the reality being one's own Self (Śaṅkara), or beyond the individual self, the Supreme being other than it (Raṅgarāmānuja). Madhva's bhāṣya, in our source, has no comment on this verse.

parallels.note: Yājñavalkya describes the imperishable to Gārgī by a longer list of absences.
Not grasped by the eye or by speech.

contemporary.text: Instruments extend the senses; they do not replace them. Whatever they measure still arrives as something like sound, touch or form. The verse points to what would remain if every such quality were taken away, and asks whether that is nothing or the one who perceives. Questions about consciousness still meet that difficulty. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Try to imagine something with no sound, touch, shape, taste or smell. What is left in your imagination?
reflect.deeper: Why does the verse describe the goal almost entirely by what it is not? What does such a description do that a positive one cannot?
reflect.practice: Sit quietly and notice, one by one, what you hear, feel, see, taste and smell. Then notice what is aware of all five.

flags.note: mahataḥ param: beyond the cosmic intellect (Śaṅkara) or beyond the individual self of 1.3.13 (Raṅgarāmānuja). Madhva's bhāṣya has no comment on the verse.
